title: Physiological Effects of Touching Wood
research_question: To clarify the physiological effects of touching wood with the palm, in comparison with touching other materials, on brain activity (prefrontal cortex oxy-Hb concentration) and autonomic nervous activity (heart rate variability).

participants.description: Female university students (mean age, 21.7 ± 1.6 years) in Japan. Excluded smokers, those in treatment for disease, and those with menstrual period during the study.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but likely from Chiba University given the research center location.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Plates of uncoated white oak, marble, ceramic tile, and stainless steel. All materials were 300 × 300 mm and had a uniform thickness of 43 mm (achieved by adhering Japanese cedar plywood underneath non-wood materials). Surfaces were brushed (white oak) or buffed (marble, tile, stainless steel), with wax applied to tile. All materials kept at room temperature (25 °C).
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Figure 3, Table 1, and '2.3. Tactile Stimulation' section

measures.instrument: Near-infrared time-resolved spectroscopy (TRS-20 system; Hamamatsu Photonics K.K.) at Fp1 and Fp2 (prefrontal cortex)
Heart rate variability (HRV) - high-frequency (HF) component, natural logarithm transformed (ln(HF))
Heart rate variability (HRV) - low-frequency (LF)/HF ratio, natural logarithm transformed (ln(LF/HF))

measures.construct: Subjective feeling (comfortable, relaxed, natural, warm-cold, uneven-flat, dry-moist)
measures.instrument: Modified semantic differential (SD) method (13-point scale with opposing adjectives)
Profile of Mood State (POMS) short version (30 questions)

mechanisms: The 'back to nature' theory: human physiological functions are best adapted to a natural environment, and exposure to nature-derived stimuli (like wood) brings humans closer to their original natural state, inducing relaxation.
Thermal properties: wood's lower thermal conductivity compared to other materials results in a warmer subjective sensation, contributing to comfort.
Surface roughness: wood's uneven surface texture is perceived differently from smooth artificial materials, potentially contributing to its 'natural' feel.
Implicit evaluation: wood, as a familiar and natural material, elicits rapid, positive implicit evaluations leading to affective responses like comfort and relaxation.
implementation_implications: Using wood in built environments (houses, furniture) can induce physiological relaxation and improve psychological well-being.
The findings support the 'moku-iku' initiative, promoting interaction with wood for improved quality of life.

tables.description: Details of materials including thickness, thermal conductivity, arithmetic average roughness, and conditioning.

limitations: The study used only non-coated wood; the influence of various coatings on physiological responses needs clarification.
The study only examined touching wood with the palm; the effect of touching with the sole of the foot (relevant for flooring) should also be examined.
The study measured only the effects of passively placing the palm on the material; the influence of active contact (e.g., stroking) on physiological responses should be clarified.

paper_metadata.title: Physiological Effects of Touching Wood
paper_metadata.journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
paper_metadata.crossref_journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This study aimed to clarify the physiological effects of touching wood with the palm, in comparison with touching other materials on brain activity and autonomic nervous activity. Eighteen female university students (mean age, 21.7  ±  1.6 years) participated in the study. As an indicator of brain activity, oxyhemoglobin (oxy-Hb) concentrations were measured in the left/right prefrontal cortex using near-infrared time-resolved spectroscopy. Heart rate variability (HRV) was used as an indicator of autonomic nervous activity. The high-frequency (HF) component of HRV, which reflected parasympathetic nervous activity, and the low-frequency (LF)/HF ratio, which reflected sympathetic nervous activity, were measured. Plates of uncoated white oak, marble, tile, and stainless steel were used as tactile stimuli. After sitting at rest with their eyes closed, participants touched the materials for 90 s. As a result, tactile stimulation with white oak significantly (1) decreased the oxy-Hb concentration in the left/right prefrontal cortex relative to marble, tile, and stainless steel and (2) increased ln(HF)-reflected parasympathetic nervous activity relative to marble and stainless steel. In conclusion, our study revealed that touching wood with the palm calms prefrontal cortex activity and induces parasympathetic nervous activity more than other materials, thereby inducing physiological relaxation.
